FEDERAL VISUAL ARTISTS RIGHTS ACT (VARA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. · Untitled No. 4

DECLARATION AND PURPOSE
This information sheet concerns a work described as A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., titled Untitled No. 4, created by Jordan Lee (the "work"). Pat Morgan is identified here as the work's current owner or possessor, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of the federal Visual Artists Rights Act, 17 U.S.C. § 106A, which gives the author of a narrowly defined category of "work of visual art" (17 U.S.C. § 101) personal rights of attribution and integrity that exist separately from copyright ownership itself. It also summarizes the federal preemption provision, 17 U.S.C. § 301(f), which addresses how § 106A relates to state-law moral-rights statutes, including California's Art Preservation Act, Cal. Civ. Code § 987, which is covered in a separate document in this corpus.

This sheet is an informational record only. It does not determine whether A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. meets § 106A's or § 101's own definition of a "work of visual art," does not determine whether any state-law right in A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. is or is not preempted by 17 U.S.C. § 301(f), and does not itself assert, waive, reserve, or enforce any right under these statutes or any other law. It is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statutes directly.

THE TWO CORE RIGHTS: ATTRIBUTION AND INTEGRITY
Separately from copyright ownership, the federal Visual Artists Rights Act, 17 U.S.C. § 106A, gives the author of a "work of visual art" two personal rights, independent of the exclusive rights that copyright itself provides under 17 U.S.C. § 106. Subsection (a) states: "Subject to section 107 and independent of the exclusive rights provided in section 106, the author of a work of visual art — (1) shall have the right— (A) to claim authorship of that work, and (B) to prevent the use of his or her name as the author of any work of visual art which he or she did not create; (2) shall have the right to prevent the use of his or her name as the author of the work of visual art in the event of a distortion, mutilation, or other modification of the work which would be prejudicial to his or her honor or reputation; and (3) subject to the limitations set forth in section 113(d), shall have the right— (A) to prevent any intentional distortion, mutilation, or other modification of that work which would be prejudicial to his or her honor or reputation, and any intentional distortion, mutilation, or modification of that work is a violation of that right, and (B) to prevent any destruction of a work of recognized stature, and any intentional or grossly negligent destruction of that work is a violation of that right."

Paragraphs (1) and (2) together make up what is commonly called the right of attribution; paragraph (3) is commonly called the right of integrity. Both belong only to the individual human author of the work, whether or not the author is also the work's copyright owner. Subsection (b) states: "Only the author of a work of visual art has the rights conferred by subsection (a) in that work, whether or not the author is the copyright owner." Whether any specific modification of A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. would be "prejudicial to [Jordan Lee's] honor or reputation," or whether A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. is a work "of recognized stature" for purposes of the destruction right, are determinations the statute leaves to be made under its own terms; this sheet does not make either determination.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "WORK OF VISUAL ART"
The rights described elsewhere in this document apply only to a work meeting the definition of "work of visual art" in 17 U.S.C. § 101. That definition states: "A 'work of visual art' is— (1) a painting, drawing, print, or sculpture, existing in a single copy, in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author, or, in the case of a sculpture, in multiple cast, carved, or fabricated sculptures of 200 or fewer that are consecutively numbered by the author and bear the signature or other identifying mark of the author; or (2) a still photographic image produced for exhibition purposes only, existing in a single copy that is signed by the author, or in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author."

The same definition then expressly excludes several categories from that coverage: "A work of visual art does not include— (A)(i) any poster, map, globe, chart, technical drawing, diagram, model, applied art, motion picture or other audiovisual work, book, magazine, newspaper, periodical, data base, electronic information service, electronic publication, or similar publication; (ii) any merchandising item or advertising, promotional, descriptive, covering, or packaging material or container; (iii) any portion or part of any item described in clause (i) or (ii); (B) any work made for hire; or (C) any work not subject to copyright protection under this title." Whether A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. falls within the included categories and outside all of the excluded ones is a determination the statute leaves to be made under its own terms; this sheet does not make that determination.

HOW LONG THE RIGHTS LAST
17 U.S.C. § 106A(d) fixes how long the attribution and integrity rights last, and the rule differs depending on when the work was created relative to the Visual Artists Rights Act's effective date. Section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, a session-law note that is not itself codified in Title 17 but is referenced directly by § 106A(d), states that the Act's provisions "take effect 6 months after the date of the enactment of this Act [Dec. 1, 1990]" — that is, on June 1, 1991.

For a work created on or after that effective date, § 106A(d)(1) states: "With respect to works of visual art created on or after the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, the rights conferred by subsection (a) shall endure for a term consisting of the life of the author." For a work created before that effective date but not yet transferred out of the author's hands as of that date, a different rule applies. Section 106A(d)(2) states: "With respect to works of visual art created before the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, but title to which has not, as of such effective date, been transferred from the author, the rights conferred by subsection (a) shall be coextensive with, and shall expire at the same time as, the rights conferred by section 106."

HOW THE RIGHTS CAN BE WAIVED
17 U.S.C. § 106A(e) states its own rule for giving up the attribution and integrity rights, distinct from the waiver rule under any state moral-rights statute. Subsection (e)(1) states: "The rights conferred by subsection (a) may not be transferred, but those rights may be waived if the author expressly agrees to such waiver in a written instrument signed by the author. Such instrument shall specifically identify the work, and uses of that work, to which the waiver applies, and the waiver shall apply only to the work and uses so identified. In the case of a joint work prepared by two or more authors, a waiver of rights under this paragraph made by one such author waives such rights for all such authors."

The statute also separates a waiver of these rights from a transfer of the work itself or of the copyright in it. Subsection (e)(2) states: "Ownership of the rights conferred by subsection (a) with respect to a work of visual art is distinct from ownership of any copy of that work, or of a copyright or any exclusive right under a copyright in that work. Transfer of ownership of any copy of a work of visual art, or of a copyright or any exclusive right under a copyright, shall not constitute a waiver of the rights conferred by subsection (a). Except as may otherwise be agreed by the author in a written instrument signed by the author, a waiver of the rights conferred by subsection (a) with respect to a work of visual art shall not constitute a transfer of ownership of any copy of that work, or of ownership of a copyright or of any exclusive right under a copyright in that work."

HOW VARA RELATES TO STATE MORAL-RIGHTS STATUTES
The Copyright Act's general preemption section, 17 U.S.C. § 301, contains a subsection addressing specifically how the Visual Artists Rights Act relates to state-law moral rights. Subsection (f)(1) states: "On or after the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, all legal or equitable rights that are equivalent to any of the rights conferred by section 106A with respect to works of visual art to which the rights conferred by section 106A apply are governed exclusively by section 106A and section 113(d) and the provisions of this title relating to such sections. Thereafter, no person is entitled to any such right or equivalent right in any work of visual art under the common law or statutes of any State."

That rule is narrower than a blanket preemption of state moral-rights law. By its own terms it reaches only rights that are "equivalent" to the § 106A rights, and only "with respect to works of visual art to which the rights conferred by section 106A apply" — that is, works meeting § 106A's and § 101's own definition described elsewhere in this document. The same subsection then expressly preserves certain state-law rights and remedies. Subsection (f)(2) states: "Nothing in paragraph (1) annuls or limits any rights or remedies under the common law or statutes of any State with respect to— (A) any cause of action from undertakings commenced before the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990; (B) activities violating legal or equitable rights that are not equivalent to any of the rights conferred by section 106A with respect to works of visual art; or (C) activities violating legal or equitable rights which extend beyond the life of the author."

Read together, § 301(f) states that state-law rights equivalent to § 106A's, in a work meeting § 106A's own "work of visual art" definition, are governed exclusively by § 106A as to conduct on or after VARA's effective date — but state law is expressly left in place, by the statute's own terms, for a cause of action from conduct that began before that effective date, for a state-law right that is not equivalent to a § 106A right, for a state-law right in a work falling outside § 106A's own "work of visual art" definition (since paragraph (f)(1) does not reach such a work at all), and for a state-law right that by its own terms extends beyond the life of the author.

That definition states: "A 'work of visual art' is— (1) a painting, drawing, print, or sculpture, existing in a single copy, in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author, or, in the case of a sculpture, in multiple cast, carved, or fabricated sculptures of 200 or fewer that are consecutively numbered by the author and bear the signature or other identifying mark of the author; or (2) a still photographic image produced for exhibition purposes only, existing in a single copy that is signed by the author, or in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author."

The same definition then expressly excludes several categories from that coverage: "A work of visual art does not include— (A)(i) any poster, map, globe, chart, technical drawing, diagram, model, applied art, motion picture or other audiovisual work, book, magazine, newspaper, periodical, data base, electronic information service, electronic publication, or similar publication; (ii) any merchandising item or advertising, promotional, descriptive, covering, or packaging material or container; (iii) any portion or part of any item described in clause (i) or (ii); (B) any work made for hire; or (C) any work not subject to copyright protection under this title." Whether A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. falls within the included categories and outside all of the excluded ones is a determination the statute leaves to be made under its own terms; this sheet does not make that determination.

17 U.S.C. § 106A(d) fixes how long the attribution and integrity rights last, and the rule differs depending on when the work was created relative to the Visual Artists Rights Act's effective date. Section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, a session-law note that is not itself codified in Title 17 but is referenced directly by § 106A(d), states that the Act's provisions "take effect 6 months after the date of the enactment of this Act [Dec. 1, 1990]" — that is, on June 1, 1991.

For a work created on or after that effective date, § 106A(d)(1) states: "With respect to works of visual art created on or after the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, the rights conferred by subsection (a) shall endure for a term consisting of the life of the author." For a work created before that effective date but not yet transferred out of the author's hands as of that date, a different rule applies. Section 106A(d)(2) states: "With respect to works of visual art created before the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, but title to which has not, as of such effective date, been transferred from the author, the rights conferred by subsection (a) shall be coextensive with, and shall expire at the same time as, the rights conferred by section 106."

17 U.S.C. § 106A(e) states its own rule for giving up the attribution and integrity rights, distinct from the waiver rule under any state moral-rights statute. Subsection (e)(1) states: "The rights conferred by subsection (a) may not be transferred, but those rights may be waived if the author expressly agrees to such waiver in a written instrument signed by the author. Such instrument shall specifically identify the work, and uses of that work, to which the waiver applies, and the waiver shall apply only to the work and uses so identified. In the case of a joint work prepared by two or more authors, a waiver of rights under this paragraph made by one such author waives such rights for all such authors."

The statute also separates a waiver of these rights from a transfer of the work itself or of the copyright in it. Subsection (e)(2) states: "Ownership of the rights conferred by subsection (a) with respect to a work of visual art is distinct from ownership of any copy of that work, or of a copyright or any exclusive right under a copyright in that work. Transfer of ownership of any copy of a work of visual art, or of a copyright or any exclusive right under a copyright, shall not constitute a waiver of the rights conferred by subsection (a). Except as may otherwise be agreed by the author in a written instrument signed by the author, a waiver of the rights conferred by subsection (a) with respect to a work of visual art shall not constitute a transfer of ownership of any copy of that work, or of ownership of a copyright or of any exclusive right under a copyright in that work."

The Copyright Act's general preemption section, 17 U.S.C. § 301, contains a subsection addressing specifically how the Visual Artists Rights Act relates to state-law moral rights. Subsection (f)(1) states: "On or after the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, all legal or equitable rights that are equivalent to any of the rights conferred by section 106A with respect to works of visual art to which the rights conferred by section 106A apply are governed exclusively by section 106A and section 113(d) and the provisions of this title relating to such sections. Thereafter, no person is entitled to any such right or equivalent right in any work of visual art under the common law or statutes of any State."

That rule is narrower than a blanket preemption of state moral-rights law. By its own terms it reaches only rights that are "equivalent" to the § 106A rights, and only "with respect to works of visual art to which the rights conferred by section 106A apply" — that is, works meeting § 106A's and § 101's own definition described elsewhere in this document. The same subsection then expressly preserves certain state-law rights and remedies. Subsection (f)(2) states: "Nothing in paragraph (1) annuls or limits any rights or remedies under the common law or statutes of any State with respect to— (A) any cause of action from undertakings commenced before the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990; (B) activities violating legal or equitable rights that are not equivalent to any of the rights conferred by section 106A with respect to works of visual art; or (C) activities violating legal or equitable rights which extend beyond the life of the author."

Read together, § 301(f) states that state-law rights equivalent to § 106A's, in a work meeting § 106A's own "work of visual art" definition, are governed exclusively by § 106A as to conduct on or after VARA's effective date — but state law is expressly left in place, by the statute's own terms, for a cause of action from conduct that began before that effective date, for a state-law right that is not equivalent to a § 106A right, for a state-law right in a work falling outside § 106A's own "work of visual art" definition (since paragraph (f)(1) does not reach such a work at all), and for a state-law right that by its own terms extends beyond the life of the author.
